content: The following are professional interpretations of the provided references: 1. Hall et al. (2005) conducted a pilot study to evaluate the effectiveness of power mobility driving training for older adults. The findings were published in Assistive Technology and highlighted the potential benefits of such training programs in improving mobility and independence among seniors. 2. Hansen, Tresse, and Gunnarsson (2004) performed a randomized controlled clinical trial to assess the impact of active wheelchair check-ups on accident reduction and maintenance improvement. Their research, published in Clinical Rehabilitation, demonstrated that regular check-ups significantly enhance safety and wheelchair upkeep. 3. Harrison et al. (2002) explored the use of virtual reality technology in assessing and training inexperienced powered wheelchair users. Their study, published in Disability & Rehabilitation, emphasized the role of virtual environments in improving user skills and confidence. 4. Hasdai, Jessel, and Weiss (1998) investigated the use of a computer simulator to train children with disabilities in operating powered wheelchairs. Published in the American Journal of Occupational Therapy, the study demonstrated the simulator's effectiveness in enhancing operational skills. 5. Hoenig et al. (2005) compared the outcomes of rehabilitation provided by expert clinicians versus usual care for manual wheelchair provision. Their clinical trial, published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society, revealed the advantages of specialized rehabilitation in improving wheelchair use. 6. Hong et al. (2018) developed the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) to evaluate the quality of mixed-methods research. This tool, registered with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office, has become a standard for assessing methodological rigor in such studies. 7. Kenyon et al. (2017) presented a case series on power mobility training for young children with multiple severe impairments. Published in Physical & Occupational Therapy in Pediatrics, the study highlighted the individualized approaches required for this population. 8. Kirby et al. (2011) demonstrated that a wheelchair workshop for medical students significantly improved their knowledge and skills. This randomized controlled trial, published in the American Journal of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, underscored the importance of hands-on training in medical education. 9. Kirby et al. (2015) examined the proportion of wheelchair users receiving skills training during rehabilitation admissions in Canada. Their findings, published in Topics in Geriatric Rehabilitation, revealed gaps in training provision and emphasized the need for standardized programs. 10. Kirby et al. (2004) evaluated the manual wheelchair-handling skills of caregivers and the impact of training. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the study highlighted the importance of caregiver training in improving wheelchair handling and user safety. 11. Kirby et al. (2016) conducted a randomized controlled trial to assess the effectiveness of a wheelchair skills training program for powered wheelchair users. Their findings, published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, demonstrated significant improvements in user skills and confidence. 12. Kirby et al. (2016) investigated the impact of manual wheelchair skills training for community-dwelling veterans with spinal cord injuries. Published in PLOS ONE, the randomized controlled trial showed that training improved independence and mobility. 13. Lennon (1991) presented a single case study on wheelchair transfer training for a stroke patient with neglect. Published in Physiotherapy Theory and Practice, the study highlighted the challenges and strategies for addressing neglect in rehabilitation. 14. Leochico and Valera (2020) reported on the use of telerehabilitation for follow-up consultations with wheelchair recipients with paraplegia in a developing country. Published in Spinal Cord Series and Cases, the case report demonstrated the feasibility and benefits of remote consultations. 15. Loomis and Boersma (1982) described case studies using verbal mediation to train right brain-damaged patients in wheelchair tasks. Published in Physiotherapy Canada, the study emphasized the role of cognitive strategies in rehabilitation. 16. MacGillivray et al. (2018) found that individualized powered wheelchair skills training improved goal satisfaction among users. Published in Disability & Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology, the study highlighted the importance of tailoring training to individual needs. 17. MacPhee et al. (2004) conducted a randomized clinical trial to evaluate a wheelchair skills training program for users undergoing initial rehabilitation. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the study demonstrated the program's effectiveness in improving skills and confidence. 18. Mathis and Gowran (2021) conducted a cross-sectional survey investigating wheelchair skills training in Ireland. Published in Disability & Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology, the study identified gaps in training provision and recommended improvements. 19. McGarry et al. (2012) evaluated the use of a smart wheelchair as a mobility training tool for children with physical disabilities. Published in Disability & Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology, the study highlighted the potential of smart technology in pediatric rehabilitation. 20. Miller et al. (2019) assessed the influence of peer-led wheelchair training on skills and participation among older adults. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the randomized controlled trial demonstrated positive clinical outcomes. 21. Morgan et al. (2017) applied a motor learning approach to train new manual wheelchair users in propulsion biomechanics. Published in the Journal of Spinal Cord Medicine, the pilot study showed improvements in propulsion efficiency and technique. 22. Mountain et al. (2010) conducted a pilot study on the ability of stroke patients to learn powered wheelchair skills. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, the study demonstrated the feasibility of training programs for this population. 23. Mountain et al. (2014) evaluated the effectiveness of powered wheelchair skills training for stroke patients in a randomized controlled trial. Published in the American Journal of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the study showed significant improvements in mobility and independence. 24. Mountain et al. (2010) presented two case reports exploring the relevance of wheelchair skills assessment and training for long-term users. Published in Disability & Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology, the study emphasized the ongoing need for skill development. 25. Nisbet (2002) assessed and trained children in the UK for powered mobility. Published in Technology and Disability, the study highlighted the importance of early intervention in developing mobility skills. 26. Ozturk and Ucsular (2011) evaluated the effectiveness of a wheelchair skills training program for community-living manual wheelchair users in Turkey. Published in Clinical Rehabilitation, the randomized controlled trial demonstrated significant improvements in user skills. 27. Pellichero et al. (2020) explored older adults' experiences with a peer-led wheelchair training program. Published in the Canadian Journal of Occupational Therapy, the study highlighted the value of peer support in skill development. 28. Post et al. (1997) examined the availability and satisfaction with services for individuals with spinal cord injuries. Published in Spinal Cord, the study identified gaps in service provision and areas for improvement. 29. Ragonesi and Galloway (2012) reported on short-term, early intensive power mobility training for an infant at risk for cerebral palsy. Published in Pediatric Physical Therapy, the case report demonstrated the potential benefits of early intervention. 30. Rice et al. (2017) investigated the short-term influence of transfer training among pediatric wheelchair users. Published in the Journal of Spinal Cord Medicine, the randomized trial showed improvements in transfer skills and independence. 31. Rice et al. (2020) conducted a pilot study on a brief fall prevention intervention for manual wheelchair users with spinal cord injuries. Published in the Journal of Spinal Cord Medicine, the study demonstrated the intervention's feasibility and potential benefits. 32. Rigot et al. (2021) evaluated the effectiveness of a web-based transfer training program for wheelchair users. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the randomized controlled trial showed significant improvements in transfer skills. 33. Routhier et al. (2012) assessed the efficacy and retention of a French-Canadian wheelchair skills training program for manual wheelchair users. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the randomized controlled trial demonstrated positive outcomes. 34. Rusek et al. (2021) analyzed inpatient rehabilitation clinicians' perspectives on manual wheelchair training. Published in Disability & Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology, the qualitative study identified barriers and opportunities for improving training programs. 35. Sakakibara et al. (2013) conducted a pilot study on wheelchair skills training to improve confidence among older adults using manual wheelchairs. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the study demonstrated the program's effectiveness. 36. Salatino et al. (2016) conducted an observational study on powered wheelchair provision in Italy. Published in Assistive Technology, the study highlighted the need for standardized practices in wheelchair provision. 37. Sarigul-Klijn et al. (2017) explored motor learning in acquiring a novel bimanual wheelchair skill after chronic stroke. Presented at the IEEE International Conference on Rehabilitation Robotics, the study demonstrated the potential of unmasking technology in skill acquisition. 38. Wong (2018) investigated the learning process for using a rear-mounted power assist for manual wheelchairs. Published in Disability & Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology, the study highlighted the challenges and benefits of this technology. 39. Sawatzky et al. (2012) conducted a pilot study on a wheelchair skills training program for children. Published in the Australian Occupational Therapy Journal, the study demonstrated the program's feasibility and benefits. 40. Smith et al. (2020) evaluated a condensed wheelchair skills training bootcamp for students. Published in Disability & Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology, the study showed improvements in self-efficacy for assessing and training wheelchair skills. 41. Smith et al. (2016) reviewed factors influencing participation in social and community activities for wheelchair users. Published in Disability & Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology, the study identified barriers and facilitators to participation. 42. Stanton et al. (1983) described an interdisciplinary approach to wheelchair transfer training for individuals with right cerebral dysfunctions. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, the study emphasized the importance of collaboration in rehabilitation. 43. Štefanac et al. (2018) examined wheelchair users' satisfaction with prescribed wheelchairs and services in Croatia. Published in Collegium Antropologicum, the study identified areas for improvement in service delivery. 44. Suzuki and Lockette (2000) conducted a client satisfaction survey of a wheelchair seating clinic. Published in Physical and Occupational Therapy in Geriatrics, the study highlighted the importance of user feedback in service improvement. 45. Tasiemski et al. (2021) evaluated the effects of a community peer-based wheelchair skills training camp in Morocco. Published in Disability & Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology, the study demonstrated the program's positive impact on skills and confidence. 46. Taylor et al. (2015) analyzed patterns in wheeled mobility skills training, equipment evaluation, and utilization. Published in Assistive Technology, the study provided insights into training practices and outcomes. 47. Toro et al. (2016) assessed the impact of the World Health Organization's 8-step wheelchair service provision model in less-resourced settings. Published in BMC Health Services Research, the cohort study demonstrated improvements in user satisfaction and function. 48. Toro-Hernandez et al. (2020) evaluated final-year occupational therapy students' knowledge of basic manual wheelchair provision in Colombia. Published in Occupational Therapy International, the study identified gaps in education and training. 49. Trefler et al. (2004) examined the outcomes of wheelchair systems intervention in long-term care facilities. Published in Assistive Technology, the study highlighted the benefits of tailored interventions for residents. 50. Van Der Scheer et al. (2016) conducted a randomized controlled trial on low-intensity wheelchair training for inactive individuals with long-term spinal cord injuries. Published in the Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine, the study demonstrated improvements in fitness and wheelchair skills. 51. Verza et al. (2006) described an interdisciplinary approach to evaluating assistive technology needs, which reduced equipment abandonment. Published in Multiple Sclerosis, the study emphasized the importance of comprehensive assessments. 52. Visagie et al. (2016) evaluated the impact of structured wheelchair services on user satisfaction and function in Zimbabwe. Published in the African Journal of Disability, the study demonstrated the benefits of structured service delivery. 53. Webster et al. (2001) investigated computer-assisted training for improving wheelchair mobility in patients with unilateral neglect. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the study demonstrated the potential of technology in rehabilitation. 54. Williams et al. (2017) explored the perspectives of basic wheelchair users on improving access to services in Kenya and the Philippines. Published in BMC International Health & Human Rights, the qualitative study identified barriers and proposed solutions. 55. The World Health Organization (2008) published guidelines on the provision of manual wheelchairs in less-resourced settings. These guidelines, developed in Geneva, Switzerland, provide a framework for improving wheelchair access and services globally. 56. Worobey et al. (2021) evaluated the effectiveness of group wheelchair skills training for individuals with spinal cord injuries. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the randomized controlled trial demonstrated significant improvements in skills and confidence. 57. Worobey et al. (2021) assessed the impact of group wheelchair maintenance training for individuals with spinal cord injuries. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the study highlighted the importance of maintenance training in enhancing wheelchair longevity and safety. 58. Worobey et al. (2021) investigated the efficacy of web-based transfer training for independent wheelchair transfers. Published in the Archives of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, the randomized controlled trial demonstrated the feasibility and benefits of online training programs.
